title: John Bosco (1815–1888)
hook: a priest who took in street boys and taught through games and kindness

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marianne Cope, who nursed Damien and carried on his work. Your line was she stayed thirty years. Which caregiver did you help? Today, a priest with a rope stretched between two trees. Day eight hundred ninety-four.

A farm boy in the hills of Piedmont, in northern Italy, has been watching the traveling acrobats at the village fairs. He goes home and practices. Juggling. Conjuring tricks. Walking on a rope tied between two trees. Before long the other children gather to watch him. And this is the deal, as he later told it in his own memoirs: the show is free, but it comes with a prayer, and with the morning's sermon, repeated from memory. The boy grew up to be a priest in Turin, and he kept the same instinct. Start where young people already are.
screen: `A BOY ON A ROPE.` → `A FREE SHOW, AND A PRAYER.` → `START WHERE THEY ARE.`

segments.voice: His name was John Bosco, Don Bosco in Italian. First, the city. Turin was growing fast, full of factories and building sites. Boys came in from the countryside looking for work and ended up on the streets, some in prison. Don Bosco visited the prisons and was struck by how young the prisoners were. He wanted to reach boys before they ended up there. Second, the oratory. He gathered them on Sundays, in fields and yards at first, for games, Mass, catechism and food. Over time it became a home, with a roof, beds, workshops where boys learned trades, and schools. Third, the method. He called it the preventive system, and he summed it up in three words, usually translated reason, religion and loving-kindness. Reason: explain, don't just command. Religion: the sacraments and prayer at the center. Loving-kindness: the boys had to be able to tell that they were loved. He wrote, in a letter from Rome, words to the effect that it is not enough to love the young; they must know they are loved. Paul says it in his first letter to the Corinthians, in the Douay-Rheims: "Charity is patient, is kind." Fourth, the family he left. To keep the work going, he founded the Salesians, named for Saint Francis de Sales, a gentle bishop. With Saint Mary Mazzarello he also founded a community of sisters for girls. The Salesians still run schools and youth centers, and the playground is still part of the plan. A priest who once walked a rope to win a crowd never stopped believing that games could be holy ground.
screen: `BOYS ON THE STREETS OF TURIN.` · `A YARD BECOMES A HOME.` · `REASON, RELIGION, LOVING-KINDNESS.` · `THE SALESIANS.` · then, large: `CHARITY IS PATIENT, IS KIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: encourage a young person. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone younger than you. A child, a teenager, a new hire, a niece, a student. Think of one good thing you've noticed about them that they may not know you noticed. A kindness, a skill, the way they keep trying. Hold it. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, simply wish them well. When the bell rings, think how you might tell them, in words they'll actually believe. The bell holds the time.
John Bosco. A priest in Turin who gathered street boys with games, schools and workshops, and founded the Salesians.
Your line: reason, faith, kindness. Today, tell one young person one specific good thing you've seen in them. Day eight hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint John Bosco's feast on January 31, and Salesian schools and youth centers often mark it with Mass, games and a festival for their students.
